Arith Magic

ArithmeticInvariantsPermutations
Game: Pick squares in a number grid and find the trick that keeps one total the same.
How to play: Choose one square in every row and every column. Press Show hint to see the hidden row and column numbers.

Operation
Look for the math

How can someone know the total of your squares before you choose them? Because the numbers hiding beside the grid do all the work.

The hidden row and column numbers

Turn on Show hint. A number sits to the left of each row and above each column. Every square is just its row number plus its column number, or their product. Clicking to the right of a hidden number's middle makes it bigger, clicking to the left makes it smaller, and dragging changes it faster — just as in the original applet. The numbers run from −100 to 100 for sums, and from 1 to 20 for products.

Why the total cannot change

Choosing one square in permutation order — exactly one in every row and every column — uses each row number once and each column number once. So for sums

(row₁ + col₁) + (row₂ + col₂) + … = (row₁ + row₂ + …) + (col₁ + col₂ + …)

and for products (row₁ × col₁) × (row₂ × col₂) × … = (row₁ × row₂ × …) × (col₁ × col₂ × …). The order of the chosen squares makes no difference: addition and multiplication are commutative, so the total is an invariant.

What the applet really checks

The applet shows the running total after every pick, and its three little faces light up once you have picked as many squares as there are rows. It does not stop you picking two squares in the same row — the cut-the-knot page is the one that asks for one in every row and every column. Two in the same row really do change the total. The logic test walks all 23,648 one-per-row-and-column choices for sizes 2 to 7, checks the product version too, and compares every control value and running total with a second transcription of the applet's own calculation.

Try a 2×2 sum board, write down the four hidden numbers, and predict the total before picking. Then switch to products and try the same trick on a friend.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
